title: Iowa’s cancer problem is scrambling the midterms
content: As the debate season kicked off in Iowa’s heated gubernatorial race, one question seemed to animate and, in some ways, unify the candidates. “What are the immediate and specific steps that you would take to combat Iowa’s cancer crisis?” the moderator asked the Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn, who both said it was a foundational issue for their campaigns — before each accusing the other of not doing enough. Two weeks later, Iowa’s elevated cancer rates and their potential links to farm pollution came up again, at a debate in the competitive race for Senate. The subject would have been unimaginable just a few years ago in Iowa, the country’s biggest corn and hog-producing state. But the role of “Big Ag” has become a political lightning rod amid what is being described as a public health crisis. Iowa suffers from the second-highest cancer rate in the US and is one of only three states where the rate is rising. For the first time, tackling the environmental causes of cancer has been included in Iowa campaign platforms for both parties. Republicans and Democrats up and down the ticket have staked out positions vowing to take on the issue. In the governor’s race, Lahn, a farmer-turned-candidate backed by the “Make America Healthy Again” wing of the GOP, and Democrat Sand , a moderate lawyer, have made campaign trail promises to clean up water and regulate chemicals. In the tight Senate race, Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Democratic State Representative Josh Turek have wrestled with the question too, both calling this month for more funding to ensure safe drinking water. This year, nearly $30 million has been spent airing more than 100 campaign ads in Iowa that mention cancer, according to AdImpact data. In the last midterms in 2022, there was just one, backed by a little under $200,000. “Nine months ago, there was no candidate talking about this except me, and now literally every candidate is featuring it in their campaign,” said Chris Jones, a long-time water quality advocate and now Democratic candidate for state agriculture secretary. Yet both parties face the awkward challenge of balancing criticism of “Big Ag” practices with Iowa’s economic reliance on the sector. On the left, Jones argues Democrats have not been bold enough to take on “Big Ag,” ceding ground to Republicans energized by MAHA. He has gone further than any of the other candidates on the ballot in calling for more regulation and a move away from dependence on corn and soybean production. “You’ve got an issue here that should be a natural issue for Democrats: Clean environment,” he told CNN. But the party was “too chicken to take this issue up,” he said. But divisions within the Republican Party dent its credibility, argues Sara Schreiber of the League of Conservation Voters, with some MAHA voters disillusioned by Trump’s unkept promises for their movement. “They want elected officials to be responsive” to their cause – health and the environment chief among them – “and they’re not just going to be partisan,” she said. Iowa’s Health Department attributes much of its soaring cancer rates to several lifestyle factors: Obesity, alcohol and smoking chief among them. But it acknowledged that environmental exposures could play a role, inflaming Iowans who see cancer in their community. Environmental advocates and some farmers highlight the concentration of nitrate from thousands of tons of livestock manure that leaks into the state’s waters as a key culprit. A state cancer report showing Iowa’s sobering rates –– the fastest-rising in the country — “was really the game changer,” for average Iowans, said Zach Smith, a farmer and founding member of the Lobe Rangers, an advocacy group that campaigns for stronger government action on environmental toxins. “This wave of momentum and energy came in. But we need to actually turn it into something meaningful with real legislation,” said Smith, an independent voter. “That’s what we’re interested in — getting the public wound up enough where they’re willing to vote.” That the state’s Republican Party has emphasized environmental issues this election speaks both to the perceived scale of the problem and the shifting political coalitions. “It used to be a kind of liberal, tree-hugger type thing,” said James Hepp, another Lobe Rangers founder and a Republican. “It had that stigma where if you talked to any environment, you were a tree hugger, but now I think you’re just an informed citizen trying to do what’s best.” Many Iowans who spoke to CNN credited the momentum to the MAHA movement, which threw its support behind Lahn, powering his surprise primary victory over the Trump-endorsed GOP Rep. Randy Feenstra. MAHA Action, a political advocacy group run by longtime Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ally and book publisher Tony Lyons, put $1.5 million towards Lahn’s campaign, and boasts that he was the PAC’s first 2026 endorsement. “MAHA was the first to believe in Zach Lahn, and the Iowa Republicans proved us right,” Lyons said in a statement. “November is where we prove we can win.” Yet there is distrust over the party’s commitment. Lahn has had to wrestle with GOP action in Washington, where the Trump administration ordered more domestic production of pesticides and rolled back a host of environmental regulations. “I was one of the first people to come out and say that this was the wrong move to sign that executive order,” on more US pesticide production, Lahn told CBS’ “Face the Nation” this month. “I think that if we could give the president the advice on that, that he would understand that better.” But David Murphy, a MAHA-aligned Democrat who supported RFK Jr.’s presidential run, says he’s skeptical of Lahn because of the disappointing Republican record on MAHA under Trump. “I fundamentally think that the Trump administration and Republicans have screwed up a major opportunity that RFK Jr. endorsed,” said Murphy, a fifth-generation Iowan who now works on Jones’ agriculture secretary campaign. In one of the most competitive Senate races in the country, allies of Turek —who was born with Spina Bifida linked to his father’s exposure to Agent Orange in Vietnam — have raised the subject to attack his Republican opponent. “Across America, cancer rates are going down, but in Iowa they’re going up. As a doctor, I cannot ignore what is happening,” says Dr. Selden Spencer of Huxley, Iowa, in an ad from a Democratic super PAC with nearly $3 million spent in airtime since September. It goes on to criticize Hinson for accepting campaign contributions from accused polluters. Hannah Goss, a spokesperson for the Turek campaign said: “Unlike Hinson, Josh Turek will work with anyone to put Iowans — not big corporations — first and finally address Iowa’s water quality crisis, crack down on the companies that pollute our water, and tackle Iowa’s cancer crisis head-on.” Hinson’s campaign did not address the claims in the ad when asked. But this week, she joined with Democratic Rep. Hillary Scholten of Michigan to introduce legislation aimed at improving access to early detection cancer screenings. “So many Iowa families have been touched by cancer, including mine. Iowa’s rising cancer rates are unacceptable, and we have to do everything we can to reverse this trend,” Hinson wrote on social media . Republicans are also grappling with internal fractures driven by the MAHA movement, when pro-business and public health interests collide. One key point of contention is glyphosate — an herbicide commonly known as RoundUp. While many Iowans believe nitrate levels from manure are causing health problems, there are significant divides over the herbicide between farmers and MAHA activists, who say it is also driving cancer rates across the country. “The reality is that we have all had a lot of exposure to glyphosate,” said Smith, “as a lot of farmers have.” Disagreement over the chemical has created a dividing line that has alienated farmers — many of whom say it is necessary to keep millions of crops safe through each farming season — from the broader MAHA message, he said. The science on glyphosate and health risks is far from definitive. The Environmental Protection Agency is undergoing a routine review of its safety this year, but the issue has been supercharged by Kennedy, who has a history fighting broad use of the pesticide. Reflecting the internal divisions, the Republican candidate for Iowa agriculture secretary, Mike Naig, has criticized Lahn, his party’s gubernatorial candidate, on the subject. “This is more complex than what some want to make it, and I think you’ve got some who have decided it’s a political issue. And I think that can be very dangerous,” he said in August. Amid fissures on the right, Democrats are leaning into the issue. It’s “ unsurprising that one of the stronger MAHA movements” emerged in Iowa given the incidence of cancer there, said Lauren French of Senate Majority PAC, the Democratic super PAC behind the ads in the Turek-Hinson race. But while the burgeoning movement is “leaning more Republican at the moment,” she sees an opening. For Democrats, talking about “Big Ag” chemicals “fits into the larger issue of corruption,” she said, nodding to another major voter concern this cycle. “The problem for Republicans in Iowa, is that they have a long history of being on the wrong side of this. They chose to align themselves with the companies that are doing the poisoning of the water,” she said. Some Democrats, however, also face scrutiny. Lahn has accused Sand of being beholden to agricultural interests and accused him of taking money from a donor “ caught polluting your drinking water” — claims vigorously contested by Sand’s campaign. In the closing weeks of the race, Sand has held a roundtable with cancer survivors in West Des Moines, discussing his plans to tackle the problem and pledging to “appoint a Cancer Task Force.” “Rob Sand is the only candidate in the race with a plan to address those concerns,” said Emma O’Brien, the deputy campaign manager. “Meanwhile, Zach Lahn supports the One Big Beautiful Bill, which cuts funding for cancer research, and wants to ban mRNA vaccines, which have been found to be a promising treatment for cancer.” Lahn’s campaign did not reply to CNN’s requests for comment. A poll released this week from the Cook Political Report, in partnership with New River Strategies and GS Strategy Group, has Sand with a clear lead over Lahn in the contest for governor. A CNN poll of polls in Iowa this week shows the Senate race in a dead heat. CNN’s Nadia Kounang and Ariel Edwards-Levy contributed to this report.
ranking_reason: Iowa's cancer problem is scrambling the midterms

analysis.reason: Iowa's cancer problem is scrambling the midterms

final_quality.reason: The article reports on a significant development in the 2022 midterms, specifically the increased attention to Iowa's cancer problem and its links to farm pollution, making it a newsworthy and important topic for readers to care about.

title: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in northeast Nigeria
content:
Unknown gunmen have raided a remote village in the northeast Nigerian state of Taraba, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police say.
There are fears the actual death toll is much higher, with eyewitnesses speaking of 20 lives lost and a non-governmental organisation suggesting a toll of as many as 50.
The gunmen reportedly swooped on the village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area mounted on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers on Friday in a rampage that went on for up to four hours.
Police say they are searching for other casualties in the bush but the authorities were accused by Amnesty International of failing to protect rural communities.
Nigeria continues to face attacks by armed groups across several regions, including the northwest, northeast and central regions.
The country is also battling a jihadist insurgency in its northeast that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of insecurity.
Following the latest incident, police said they recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call.
The attackers had fled by the time they arrived but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, they told BBC News on Saturday.
"We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen though there was no casualty on their side and ours because the terrain is difficult and they're used to the terrain," Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said.
He added that officers were continuing to search the bush nearby for people who might have been killed or wounded, and warned the death toll could still rise.
Speaking to AFP news agency, community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi said the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece.
"They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions," he said. "They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack."
Survivors who spoke to AFP said they had counted at least 20 dead.
"People were running in different directions to escape the attack," Binnari resident Isiyaku Musa said. "Nobody knew where it was safe to go."
Another survivor, Sa'idu Nuhu, said that some people were still missing.
Amnesty's Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, told BBC News on Saturday that the NGO had spoken to some of the bereaved families who said up to 50 people had died.
"The initial funeral had 37 people," he said.
Sanusi called for an impartial investigation into the killings, accusing the authorities of leaving rural communities "at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity".
Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent.
ranking_reason: Major political significance, significant human consequences, and moderate global reach.

title: Ramaswamy and Trump gamble on an incendiary ad, as Ohio shows signs it might turn purple again
content: Vivek Ramaswamy is ending his run for Ohio governor the same way he launched himself onto the political scene four years ago — with a bet that voters will reward him for a never-back-down bombast that mirrors President Donald Trump’s instincts. But interviews with voters over three days following the release of the Republican nominee’s ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, offered a glimpse at the potential perils of imitating Trump — particularly in a year in which polls show voters turning away from the president. And if Ramaswamy’s approach alienates enough moderate and independent voters, a Republican Party looking for its way forward in the fast-approaching post-Trump era could find itself losing the ground it gained in a state that not long ago was a perpetual political battleground. The ad at issue shows Acton’s estranged mother calling her own daughter a liar and urging voters to reject her. Acton has said she hasn’t seen her mother since she was 12 years old, when her mother lost custody of her children. Her stepfather was indicted by a grand jury on charges of sexually abusing her. Confronted on those underlying details this week, both Trump and Ramaswamy deflected and pointed to the mother’s allegations. In CNN’s conversations with voters after the ad was published, the dynamics in the governor’s race felt similar to those playing out nationally: Die-hard Republicans who still support Trump remain strongly in Ramaswamy’s camp, despite the controversy. They remain angry at Acton over her role in Ohio’s Covid-19 response, a period in which she was director of the Ohio Department of Health, and say both campaigns have aired negative ads. More moderate and independent voters, though, said they were bothered by the ad, and that it does change how they see the GOP nominee. The question that could decide the governor’s race in a state Trump won by 11 percentage points in 2024 is just how many Republicans Ramaswamy is able to keep in his camp as the controversy engulfs the race’s final days. Kari Freudenberger, a 47-year-old substitute teacher and social worker from Madeira who described herself as independent, said after seeing Ramaswamy speak Wednesday in Cincinnati that the ad was “heinous and horrible” — and makes her less likely to vote for the biotech entrepreneur. “I don’t care if Ramaswamy’s policies are the best. That shows a judgment of character that I don’t want to see anymore in politics,” she said. Cherise Wilson, a 48-year-old nurse who lives near Cincinnati and said she is a Republican, told CNN she is “torn” about the governor’s race — and on whether it was appropriate to use Acton’s mother in an ad. “I feel bad for Amy in the sense that she was truly a victim,” she said. “But I also don’t want somebody running the state of Ohio who is a victim and is in victim mode. … But I also don’t want somebody who is going to be a complete — can I say a**?” An independent voter who asked not to be named, a 57-year-old chemist who came to the rally because he works nearby, said he was impressed by Ramaswamy’s 2024 presidential campaign and initially excited he was running for governor of Ohio. But he said he’s been turned off by the advertising in the race — including Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Acton’s mother. He is now unsure who he’ll vote for. “I just feel like you don’t even need that stuff,” he said. “The ads are a real turnoff on both sides.” The ad was met with immediate criticism , including from the man Ramaswamy is running to replace, two-term Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. “The ad on its face is deeply, deeply troubling,” DeWine told reporters Thursday. “But when you know the rest of the story … it makes it just more wrong.” But prominent Republicans, including Trump and Vice President JD Vance, have defended Ramaswamy and the ad. Trump on Friday said even knowing Acton’s history, Ramaswamy should continue airing the ad . “A mother is saying, ‘Don’t put my daughter there because she’s a terrible person and she’s a liar,’” Trump said. “Why shouldn’t somebody use that?” Ramaswamy, at an event on Friday and later when speaking to reporters, claimed that “our ad had nothing, nothing to do with childhood abuse, sexual abuse” — ignoring Acton’s history, which she had described publicly before the ad. When pushed by CNN about whether he harbored doubts that Acton was abused by her stepfather, Ramaswamy deflected, noting he had never met or spoken to Acton’s mother and repeating his previous attack on Acton’s credibility. “I think that in the standard of political advertising that they have used and that the media regularly accepts, I think it is absolutely acceptable for voters to hear and make a decision for themselves,” he said. Ramaswamy’s approach to the controversy was a reminder of his pugnacious bid for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination. Several other candidates were willing to criticize Trump, frequently and sharply, in speeches and on debate stages, even through Trump chose not to appear. Ramaswamy, by contrast, was often the president’s most vocal defender. He sought the limelight and relished clashes with other candidates, often talking over and insulting them in a style reminiscent of Trump’s 2015 rise. The irony of the explosive chapter in the Ohio governor’s race is that it kicked off when the ad was first published not by Ramaswamy’s campaign, but by an Ohio political blogger, D.J. Byrnes, who is known as “The Rooster.” Byrnes told CNN he obtained the video from a voter who saw it as part of a poll and recorded it. After the video leaked Monday night, Ramaswamy’s campaign was at a crossroads. Should it distance itself or take responsibility and lean into the incendiary line of attack? It wasn’t until shortly before 2 p.m. Tuesday that the campaign broke its silence on the ad, and even then, its statement did not say whether it was responsible for the spot. About five hours later, Ramasawmy ended the mystery. “It is an ad from our campaign,” he told reporters after a town hall in the Columbus area. By the end of the evening, his campaign had announced it would spend $4 million to run the ad, making clear it would not back down. At campaign stops Friday, Republicans who had lined up to see Ramaswamy said they were going to continue to support him — even if they had misgivings about the ad. Joan Smith, who was waiting outside a pancake breakfast with Ramaswamy in Strongsville, said she is “not happy about” the ad and hopes Ramaswamy’s campaign will take the ad off the air. “But I’m not going to throw the baby out with the bath water,” she said. “Politics is a dirty game. You can’t be weak in something like this.” Still, she said, the ad was “a shocker.” “It’s bad. I don’t like it. That wasn’t necessary,” she said. “But he did it and it’s over, and people make mistakes all the time, and I don’t think he should have done that.” At the same event, Joyce Tedrick said she had “no concerns” about the ad. “I think it just goes along with the fact that she isn’t always truthful,” she said. “It’s too bad.”
ranking_reason: The controversy surrounding the ad may have significant consequences for the Ohio governor's race and the Republican Party's standing in the state.

analysis.reason: The controversy surrounding the ad may have significant consequences for the Ohio governor's race and the Republican Party's standing in the state.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant development in the Ohio governor's race, specifically the controversy surrounding an ad that may have major consequences for the Republican Party's standing in the state. The article provides a clear reason for readers to care, offering insight into the dynamics of the race and the potential impact on the GOP's future in Ohio.
